> 1. Is it ok ok recommend AES-256 without specifying the mode? I do not think FIPS approves of AES-256 for all modes. For example, certain modes like ECB are generally not recommended by FIPS.

It is restricted, though - there's a whole section that says what modes are approved, recommended, and prohibited. Perhaps it's worth familiarising yourself with the whole document.

> 2. AES under 256 bit key length has problems with quantum resistance. When you apply grovers algorithm to symmetric crypto, you effective 1/2 the bit size. Quantum computing is coming and fast. I suggest we at least warm about this.

AES128 and AES192 are at the bottom of the list. The blurb used to say 'ordered from most to least preferred' but that has gone, but the list order does strongly imply "top first". They have to be present in order to accommodate a lot of legacy tech that should be cycled out by the time quantum computing is cryptographically relevant (earliest expert estimate for that is still 5yrs away). 

> 3. This is likely the wrong place to post this, can you suggest a better place?

Regarding the 'why tables' comment, I mean, why not? It presents the information in a useful and portable way, and is much more functional that bullet points. It keeps the formatting consistent, and allows us to add extra information (e.g. references, specifications, relevant notes, etc.).

I want to reiterate that there is absolutely no need to use an AES key size smaller than 256 bits. 

Suggesting it for new development is not just unnecessary—it’s a security risk. For several reasons, we should remove it from consideration and classify it as legacy.

With modern hardware (especially AES-NI and other hardware accelerations), the performance overhead of AES-256 compared to AES-128 is negligible. This is the typical scenario in web apps and API's.

Also, Grover’s algorithm effectively halves the security strength of symmetric ciphers in a quantum context:
	•	AES-128 → 64-bit security (potentially insecure in a post-quantum world)
	•	AES-256 → 128-bit security (still considered secure against quantum attacks)

I strongly believe AES-256 (with a good mode) should be the default choice for all new development, regardless of what FIPS says.
